title: Association between fluoridated toothpaste use and dental caries in Nigeria: A systematic review and meta-analysis
content:
by Adetayo Aborisade, Amina Mohammed Ali, Mcking Amedari, Abideen Olurotimi Salako, Folahanmi Tomiwa Akinsolu, Olunike Rebecca Abodunrin, Oluwabukola Mary Ola, Mobolaji Timothy Olagunju, George Uchenna Eleje, Joanne Lusher, Oliver Chukwujekwu Ezechi, Moréniké Oluwátóyìn Foláyan

Fluoride-containing dentifrices reduce dental caries risk. This systematic review addressed two questions: (i) the prevalence and frequency of fluoridated toothpaste use among Nigerian children and adolescents across geographic and demographic settings, and (ii) its association with caries prevalence, stratified by location and baseline caries risk. Registered with PROSPERO (CRD42022362116) and reported per PRISMA, the review used a PIO framework including children/adolescents aged 6 months–19 years in Nigeria who used fluoridated toothpaste, with caries measured by dmft/DMFT. PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, AJOL, and Google Scholar were searched from January 2001 to January 2026, supplemented by reference and grey-literature searches. Multiple reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias; inter-rater reliability was high. Data were pooled using random-effects models, with sensitivity, subgroup, and meta-regression analyses exploring heterogeneity and effect modifiers. Publication bias was assessed via funnel plots and Egger’s test. From 1,194 records, 18 studies (n = 12,719 participants) were included. Fluoridated toothpaste use was widespread (61.9%–95.8%), but its association with caries varied by location. Meta-analysis of 14 studies showed a 16% reduction in caries odds after removing an influential outlier (OR=0.84, 95% CI 0.71–0.99, p = 0.04). Subgroup analyses found 26% lower odds in mixed dentition and 13% lower odds in permanent dentition, with no effect in primary dentition. Hospital-based studies reported 41% lower odds among users; population-based studies showed a 5% reduction. All studies had low risk of bias, and no significant publication bias was detected. Fluoridated toothpaste use is highly prevalent in Nigeria and findings suggest possible association with lower caries experience. However, variability across residential settings and observational evidence preclude firm causal conclusions. Further longitudinal, well-controlled studies are needed to confirm the extent and consistency of this association and clarify the influence of residential location and other factors.
